title: Perf regression bisect & canary notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a living note for investigating serving-runtime performance regressions. Focus areas: profiling bottlenecks, reliable bisect workflows, and canary vs production comparisons. Use this during triage, RCA and when drafting perf-focused PRs.

When to use this doc:
- Alerts indicate increased latency p95/p99, throughput drops, or elevated GPU CPU/memory utilization after a deploy or infra change.
- Canary shows divergence from baseline (higher tail latency, lower tokens/sec).
- We suspect a code or dependency change impacting kernels, batching, or KV cache.

Quick triage checklist (first 15 minutes):
1) Confirm scope: single model, model family, region, or global. Check canary vs prod dashboards.
2) Note time window and correlated deploys (check CI/CD, rollout IDs).
3) Capture baseline metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, batch sizes, GPU utilization, host CPU, network I/O.
4) Check error rates and backpressure (queue length, timeouts).
5) If deploy suspected: flag the rollout and optionally rollback canary.
6) Start a bisect if change set unknown.

Dashboards & panels to open immediately:
- Serving Runtime Perf Overview (p50/p95/p99 latency by model & route)
- Throughput dashboard (tokens/sec, requests/sec, batch size distribution)
- Hardware utilization (GPU util, GPU mem alloc, CPU load, host memory, PCIe bandwidth)
- Batching & queue metrics (waiting workers, batch build time, dropped requests)
- KV cache hit/miss rate and prefix cache stats
- Canary comparison dashboard (side-by-side baseline vs canary)
- Recent deploys & rollout timeline (CI links)

Common failure modes & quick signals:
- Increased p95 with unchanged GPU util => likely queuing or cold-starts (batches smaller, increased scheduling overhead).
- Increased GPU util but latency also up => kernel regression or bigger model variant selected.
- Sudden drop in tokens/sec, GPU idle with high queue length => throttling or scheduler deadlock.
- Increase in host CPU and system time => serialization/deserialization overheads or data pre-processing changes.
- Memory pressure leading to OOMs / increased GC => new buffers or larger KV-resident state.

Bisect workflow (code-level):
- Goal: isolate commit/PR that introduced regression. Use binary search on deploys.
- Preconditions: reproducible perf delta on a stable workload (use recorded trace or synthetic steady workload).
- Steps:
  1) Reproduce on current canary and record metrics (baseline: last-known-good commit + current-head).
  2) Identify candidate deploys between last-good and head from rollout timeline.
  3) Use bisect helper scripts (infra/bisect.sh) to spin up short-lived instances with selected commits or cherry-picks. If infra heavy, prefer testing locally with the same model config + synthetic traffic.
  4) For each test commit: run steady-state workload for N minutes (recommend 10m warmup + 20m measurement). Collect p50/p95, tokens/sec, GPU util, batch-size histogram, KV hit rate.
  5) Compare statistically (see "Stat tests" below) and mark commit as good/bad. Continue binary search until candidate commit found.
  6) Once isolated, run perf profiler on that commit and previous commit to capture diff.

Bisect tips:
- Use the same instance type and model config to avoid confounding.
- Ensure deterministic seeds for synthetic requests if using sampling.
- If multiple commits change unrelated subsystems (e.g., infra vs runtime), prioritize runtime or anything touching batching, kernel selection, or compilation.

Canary comparison methodology (production vs canary):
- Run canary and baseline in parallel for at least 1 hour under representative traffic. Longer for tail metrics.
- Metrics to compare: p50, p90, p95, p99 latency, tokens/sec, batch size distribution, error rate, GPU util, host CPU sys time, queue length.
- Use percent-change and absolute difference. For tail metrics prefer relative increase thresholds + absolute floor (e.g., p95 increase > 20% AND delta > 20ms).
- Statistical tests: bootstrap p95 distributions or use Welch's t-test on transformed metrics (log-latency). For p99 use non-parametric rank tests or bootstrap CI.
- Minimum sample size: aim for >1000 requests per model variant for p95 stability; for p99 aim for >10k if possible.
- Watch for sampling bias: if canary receives different traffic mix, tag and compare per-route/model subset.

Automated alerts and thresholds (examples we use):
- p95 latency increase > 25% sustained for 5m => page SRE on-call.
- tokens/sec drop > 20% sustained for 10m => alert to eng-serving-runtime channel.
- batch-size 50th percentile drops by >30% (with queue >0) => investigate batching regression.
- GPU mem alloc increase > 10% vs baseline => investigate model artifacts or memory growth.

Alert triage playbook (mapping alerts -> quick likely causes):
- Latency (tail) + normal GPU util -> queuing, smaller batches, scheduler regression. Check batch-size histogram and queue length.
- Latency + high GPU util + high kernel time -> kernel change / different quantization path. Check recent model compilation flags, kernel versions.
- tokens/sec drop + GPU idle + queue growth -> throttling or worker deadlock. Investigate thread pools, backpressure signals.
- Spikes in host CPU + serialization time -> input preprocessing regressions or increased data copying.

Profiling checklist (what to run after isolating candidate commit):
- CPU profile (perf or py-spy) during steady-state traffic.
- GPU timeline / nvprof / Nsight (or our in-house tracing) for kernels showing high time.
- Kernel-level metrics: FLOPs, memory bandwidth, kernel launches per token.
- Runtime traces: end-to-end span breakdown (enqueue, batch-build, decode, token emit).
- Batch-construct timeline: per-request waiting time vs kernel-exec time.

Runbook for incidents (step-by-step):
1) Acknowledge alert and record CMD: timestamp, alert name, scope, initial triage lead.
2) Snapshot dashboards & collect traces (Grafana links, jaeger traces).
3) If it's canary-only: pause or rollback the rollout. If prod-affecting, consider short rollback to last-known-good while investigating.
4) Bisect to identify suspect commit(s).
5) Apply mitigations: revert PR, add guardrails (rate-limit), increase capacity, or tune batching parameters.
6) Post-incident: collect artifacts for postmortem (bisect log, profiles, grafana snapshots, GH PRs).

Postmortem capture checklist:
- Root cause summary (code/infra change).
- Detection timeline and MTTR.
- Contributing factors (missing alerts, test gaps).
- Concrete actions and owners (e.g., add perf unit test, add canary gates, change rollout config).
- Verify fix: run regression harness and staggered canary with stricter metrics.

Known playbook examples (short):
- Small-tail latency regression after runtime bump -> found kernel selection flag changed default. Fix: pin kernel-selection flag and add unit perf test.
- Canary memory growth -> new feature allocated buffer per request. Fix: reuse buffer pool + add mem regression alert.

- TODO: add perf unit tests that exercise batching logic under varied request shapes.

Appendix: commands & helpers:
- infra/bisect.sh --commit-range --model --instance-type --duration
- tools/perf-collect --run-id --out=./artifacts/<run-id> --metrics p50,p95,p99,tokens_per_sec,gpu_util,batch_hist
- scripts/compare_canary.py --baseline <prom-id> --canary <prom-id> --metrics p95,p99 --bootstrap

Example incident note (short):
- 2026-02-12 10:23 UTC: p95 prod increased 32% after rollout r-2026-02-12-09. Reproduced locally. Bisect identified PR#678 which changed kernel fallback ordering. Reverted PR, metrics returned to baseline. Action: add perf test and restrict kernel fallback on rollout.

If you add findings, please append notes here with timestamps and links to artifacts.
